amalgamation

/uh-mal-guh-MAY-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Amalgamation means the process or result of blending separate, distinct things — traditions, substances, or organizations — into one new whole.

Modern English is an amalgamation of Anglo-Saxon, Norse, Norman French, and Latin, each conquest and contact folding new vocabulary into a single language.

Example

The new engineering firm is an amalgamation of three small companies — one known for bridges, one for tunnels, and one for software — blended into a single team with one name and one payroll.

Three formerly separate companies with distinct specialties have been combined into one new organization, and amalgamation names exactly that result of merging different parts into a single whole.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

blend: A blend is a smooth combining in which the parts soften into each other — a blended coffee, a blended tone. An amalgamation insists the sources were genuinely distinct — different traditions, companies, languages — before they were folded into one new whole. Similar things blend easily; an amalgamation unites true differents.

composite: A composite is a whole assembled from parts that keep doing their separate jobs, like a composite photo or a composite material. An amalgamation goes further: its ingredients are blended into one new thing rather than fitted together, so the joints stop mattering.

synthesis: A synthesis is the deliberate combining of ideas or findings into a new whole, and it lives mostly in the world of thought — a synthesis of two theories. An amalgamation can merge anything — firms, styles, languages — and stresses the blended result more than the reasoning.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

separation: the state of being kept apart

division: the splitting of one thing into parts

Where it sits · how completely the parts merge — mixture → amalgamation → fusion

mixture vs. amalgamation: Mixture is weaker: in a mixture the ingredients sit together but stay recognizably separate, while an amalgamation blends them into one new whole.

fusion vs. amalgamation: Fusion is stronger: an amalgamation still lets a careful eye trace the original parts, but a fusion melts them together so completely that no seams remain.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — amalgam

Root — amalgam: a blended mass; originally an alloy of mercury with another metal (Medieval Latin amalgama, origin uncertain — possibly Arabic al-malgham or Greek malagma, "soft mass")

Suffix — -ation

Suffix — -ation: noun-forming: the act, process, or result of

Put it together

Put it together: An amalgam was originally metal blended with mercury into a single alloy; add -ation and you get the act or result of blending distinct things into one — the word's meaning kept the image and left the chemistry behind.

Use the root in a new word: amalgamate

Use the root in a new word: amalgamate: The two rival student newspapers voted to amalgamate into a single weekly publication.

Word Building

Word Choice

Formal — history, culture, and institutional writing

Amalgamation stresses that genuinely distinct things — traditions, languages, organizations — have been blended into one new whole; the word originally named the blending of metals with mercury into an alloy. Reach for it when the sources differ from one another and the result is a single unified thing rather than a loose collection sitting side by side.
